items.raw_snippet: # Big Tech Companies Mobilize Funding for AI Infrastructure. Meta, Google, and Amazon use rights offerings, bonds, IPOs to fund AI infrastructure amid rising costs. U.S. big tech companies are mobilizing large-scale funding for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure investments, utilizing methods such as rights offerings, corporate bond issuances, initial public offerings (IPOs), and revenue generation through paid services. On the 5th (local time), the Financial Times (FT) cited multiple sources reporting, “Meta’s management is considering a rights offering to address increased capital expenditure (CAPEX) for AI this year.” This is to secure funds for massive AI investments. Meta plans to invest up to US$145 billion (approximately 226 trillion Korean won) in AI infrastructure this year. Amazon plans to invest US$200 billion in AI infrastructure this year, while Google has announced up to US$190 billion, signaling astronomical-scale investments by major tech players. Anthropic and OpenAI’s rush to go public is also driven by the need for funds for AI infrastructure investments.

items.snippet: 投资银行高盛认为，当前人工智能（AI）热潮仅仅是华尔街的一次大规模交易行为而非革命。
items.raw_snippet: Goldman Sachs, the mega investment bank, reckons that AI is just *“one big trade on the US economy”.* And the AI investment bubble is getting even larger. In the last week, the AI model maker, Anthropic, announced that it was issuing shares to potential investors in what is called in stock market jargon, an Initial Public Offering (IPO). And yet SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic are all currently loss-making and the commercial potential of AI models and, in the case of Space X in going to Mars, remains unknown. AI is one big trade for the US stock market investors and one big bet on the US economy. That’s because the amount of capital investment being made by the companies called the ‘hyperscalers’ into AI models, data centres and other AI equipment is staggering. If this starts to drop, the US economy will enter recession very quickly — even if tech investments decline only by a little bit, say 4 to 6 per cent, as happened after much smaller tech booms in the 1960s and during the 2009 recession.

items.raw_snippet: # Jim Cramer sees one bright spot in the AI funding crunch. Money has a way of feeling infinite right up until the moment someone asks you to count it. It assumes the cash to pay for all of this is just sitting there, waiting, in some account no one ever has to drain. Cramer's worry is not complicated, which is part of why it sticks. He counted roughly $80 billion for Alphabet, then about $100 billion each for Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX and Amazon, and asked whether the market really holds $500 billion in "spare change" to absorb the lot, he wrote in a June 2 post on X. That is the same arithmetic he laid out when he did the math on five mega-IPOs and concluded the numbers do not add up, as seen in my TheStreet report. The wall of money Cramer worries about is also a wall of money that, so far, keeps showing up when the deals are good.

items.raw_snippet: As the AI bull run threatens formerly high-growth sectors like software, investors seek safety in HALO companies out of the tech’s reach. Photo illustration of four pillars with a plane, light bulb, construction cones, and a house on each one, and halos on top of them. ## Sign up for smart news, insights, and analysis on the biggest financial stories of the day. HALO, an acronym for heavy assets, low obsolescence, refers to a trade that confers a degree of *immunity*. Immunity from the potentially corrosive effects of AI on some assets, that is. As the artificial intelligence bull run that’s lifted markets threatens formerly high-growth sectors like software with painful disruption, traders are seeking investments that can arguably sidestep or withstand AI and, in some cases, even benefit from it. The opposite of this, what’s not HALO, are companies that are *capital light*, having minimal physical inventory or physical assets.
